description: We're building a system that fuses NASA satellite data (SMAP, POWER, MODIS) with low-cost soil sensors, so one sensor can correct NASA estimates for nearby farms, even those without sensors. The result: simple crop-suitability advice for small farmers. We're looking for teammates with skills in: hardware/IoT (ESP32, sensors), data analysis (Python, remote sensing), UI/UX design, or agronomy knowledge. Passionate about sustainable agriculture? Join us!

details:
Digital Ibis – Smart Agriculture Powered by NASA Data and Ground Sensors

**What does the project do and how does it work?**

Digital Ibis is a smart agriculture project designed to help farmers make better decisions about soil conditions, crop suitability, and sustainable crop rotation. It combines NASA Earth observation data, environmental information, crop requirements, and ground-level measurements from a proposed integrated agricultural sensor station.

The station is designed to measure soil moisture, soil temperature, electrical conductivity (EC), and pH, along with weather conditions such as air temperature, humidity, wind speed, wind direction, and rainfall. These measurements complement satellite observations by providing information about actual conditions at the field location.

The collected information is intended to be processed and analyzed through an AI-powered decision-support system. The system aims to evaluate field conditions, assess crop suitability, and generate understandable agricultural recommendations. An application MVP demonstrates how farmers can interact with the proposed solution and access its insights.

**What are its benefits and expected impacts?**

Digital Ibis aims to bridge the gap between large-scale satellite observations and real field conditions. It could help farmers make more informed crop-selection and crop-rotation decisions, improve awareness of soil and environmental conditions, and support more efficient use of agricultural resources. Its location-based design is intended to make it adaptable to agricultural land in different regions worldwide.

**What tools, software, programming languages, and hardware were used?**

The project development includes NASA Earth observation and environmental data sources, agricultural datasets, an application MVP, and a conceptual 3D design of the sensor station. The proposed hardware architecture includes an ESP32 microcontroller, a TEROS 12 soil sensor, a separate pH probe, an SHT31 temperature and humidity sensor, wind sensors, a tipping-bucket rain gauge, data storage, 4G connectivity, and a solar power system.

AI-assisted tools were used to support research, organize technical information, and develop project documentation and visual design concepts. The exact programming languages and software frameworks depend on the tools used by the application and development teams.

**What new skills did the team learn?**

Through this project, the team developed skills in researching NASA Earth observation resources, understanding agricultural and environmental datasets, designing sensor-based monitoring systems, exploring AI-assisted decision support, developing application prototypes, and communicating technical ideas through 3D visualization and documentation.

**What challenges did the team face?**

One of the main challenges was integrating multiple data sources that differ in spatial resolution, temporal frequency, and measurement formats. Another challenge was designing a system that can adapt to different geographical locations rather than depending on data from a single country. The team also considered the technical challenges of sensor compatibility, calibration, data quality, and combining ground measurements with satellite observations. Developing a meaningful AI-based recommendation approach while ensuring that its outputs are scientifically supported is another important challenge.

Digital Ibis brings these elements together in a unified concept that connects Earth observation, ground sensing, AI-assisted analysis, and a farmer-facing application to support more informed and sustainable agricultural decisions.
